sectionTitle: Carbon dioxide and methane as greenhouse gases

specStatements.text: Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere maintain temperatures on Earth high enough to support life. Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases.
Students should be able to describe the greenhouse effect in terms of the interaction of short and long wavelength radiation with matter.
Some human activities increase the amounts of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. These include:
carbon dioxide
methane.
Students should be able to recall two human activities that increase the amounts of each of the greenhouse gases carbon dioxide and methane.

Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists believe that human activities will cause the temperature of the Earth’s atmosphere to increase at the surface and that this will result in global climate change.

However, it is difficult to model such complex systems as global climate change. This leads to simplified models, speculation and opinions presented in the media that may be based on only parts of the evidence and which may be biased.
Students should be able to:
evaluate the quality of evidence in a report about global climate change given appropriate information
describe uncertainties in the evidence base
recognise the importance of peer review of results and of communicating results to a wide range of audiences.
An increase in average global temperature is a major cause of climate change.
There are several potential effects of global climate change.
Students should be able to:
describe briefly four potential effects of global climate change
discuss the scale, risk and environmental implications of global climate change.
The carbon footprint is the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.
The carbon footprint can be reduced by reducing emissions of carbon dioxide and methane.
Students should be able to:
describe actions to reduce emissions of carbon dioxide and methane
give reasons why actions may be limited.

scopeNotes.statement: Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the three gases the specification names are taught as greenhouse gases. No other greenhouse gases (for example nitrous oxide or CFCs) are introduced, and the specification is not extended into ozone depletion or into acid rain, so sulfur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen and carbon monoxide appear only as distractors that are explicitly corrected, never as taught greenhouse gases.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to recall two human activities that increase the amounts of each of the greenhouse gases carbon dioxide and methane.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The requirement is recall of two activities per gas, so the content gives a small, standard set (fossil fuel combustion and deforestation for carbon dioxide; livestock farming, rice growing in flooded fields and decomposition of waste in landfill for methane). No exhaustive inventory of sources and no quantitative emission data are demanded, because the specification asks only for two per gas.

scopeNotes.statement: Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists believe that human activities will cause the temperature of the Earth’s atmosphere to increase at the surface and that this will result in global climate change.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification's own qualified wording is kept: the position is attributed to many scientists and grounded in peer-reviewed evidence, rather than being asserted as proof or presented as personal opinion. No item requires students to endorse or reject the position beyond describing how the evidence is judged.

scopeNotes.statement: There are several potential effects of global climate change.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Effects are stated as potential throughout. No item asks students to predict that a named effect will certainly happen, or by how much, because the specification says potential rather than certain.

scopeNotes.statement: describe briefly four potential effects of global climate change
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Effects are described briefly, as the specification directs. The underlying atmospheric physics, ocean chemistry and detailed ecological mechanisms behind each effect are not taught, and no item requires them.

scopeNotes.statement: The carbon footprint is the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Carbon footprint is treated qualitatively, as a definition to be applied to a life cycle. The specification sets no calculation here, so no item asks students to compute a carbon footprint value or to convert other greenhouse gases into carbon dioxide equivalents.

concepts.definition: A gas in the atmosphere that absorbs long wavelength radiation emitted by the Earth and re-radiates some of it back towards the surface. Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases.
The specification names water vapour, carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4) as greenhouse gases. Nitrogen and oxygen, which make up most of the air, are not greenhouse gases.

concepts.term: why greenhouse gases matter for life
concepts.definition: Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere maintain temperatures on Earth high enough to support life. Without them the surface would be far colder, so the natural greenhouse effect is necessary, not harmful in itself.

Short wavelength radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the Earth's surface, warming it. The warmed surface emits long wavelength radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb this long wavelength radiation and re-radiate it in all directions, including back towards the surface, keeping the Earth warmer than it would otherwise be.
Radiation from the Sun, which includes visible light and ultraviolet. It passes through the atmosphere largely unabsorbed and is absorbed by matter at the Earth's surface.
Infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface after it has been warmed. It is this longer wavelength radiation, not the incoming short wavelength radiation, that greenhouse gases absorb.

Greenhouse gas molecules absorb long wavelength radiation and then emit radiation again in all directions. They do not act as a mirror reflecting radiation straight back, and they do not stop sunlight entering.

concepts.term: human activities and greenhouse gas amounts
concepts.definition: Some human activities increase the amounts of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. The specification names carbon dioxide and methane as the gases whose amounts are increased in this way.

concepts.term: human activities that increase carbon dioxide
concepts.definition: Burning fossil fuels (for example in power stations, vehicles and homes) and deforestation. Two such activities must be recalled.

Cutting down and often burning large areas of forest. It increases atmospheric carbon dioxide in two ways: burning the timber releases carbon dioxide, and fewer trees remain to remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis.
Farming livestock such as cattle, growing rice in flooded paddy fields, and decomposition of waste in landfill sites. Two such activities must be recalled.
Methane, CH4, is released when organic material decomposes where there is little or no oxygen, such as in landfill sites and flooded rice fields, and from the digestion of food by cattle.

concepts.term: the scientific position on climate change
concepts.definition: Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists believe that human activities will cause the temperature of the Earth's atmosphere to increase at the surface, and that this will result in global climate change.

The checking of results and conclusions by other scientists working in the same field before the work is published. It helps to detect errors and false claims, so peer-reviewed evidence carries more weight than an unchecked claim.
The scientific position rests on measurements and data that have been published and checked, rather than on the personal views of individual scientists.
Global climate is a very complex system, so it is difficult to model. Models must be simplified, which means their predictions of future climate carry uncertainty.

concepts.term: speculation and opinion in the media
concepts.definition: Reports in the media may go beyond the evidence, presenting speculation and opinion. They may be based on only parts of the evidence and may be biased.

A report is biased when it presents only the evidence that supports one view, for example because of who wrote it or who paid for it. Bias makes a report less trustworthy even if the data it quotes are real.

Stronger evidence has been collected over a long period, is repeatable and reproducible, has been peer reviewed, comes from a source without a vested interest, and is reported in full rather than selectively.

Uncertainty arises because temperatures from the distant past are estimated indirectly rather than measured, records cover a short time compared with the age of the Earth, climate varies naturally, and models are simplified. Uncertainty is not the same as scientists doubting that warming is happening.

concepts.term: communicating results to a wide range of audiences
concepts.definition: Findings must reach the public, industry and governments, not only other scientists, so that people can understand the evidence and make informed decisions about how to act on it.
The mean surface temperature of the Earth, averaged over the whole planet and over time. An increase in average global temperature is a major cause of climate change.
A change in long-term patterns of temperature, rainfall and weather across the world. It does not simply mean that everywhere becomes uniformly warmer.

concepts.term: potential effects of global climate change
concepts.definition: Four that can be described briefly: rising sea levels leading to flooding and coastal erosion; more frequent and more severe storms; changes to the amount, timing and distribution of rainfall, causing drought or flooding; and changes to the distribution of wild species and to the crops that regions can grow, affecting food production.

The effects are global in scale and would affect large numbers of people and habitats, so even effects that are uncertain carry serious risk. Discussing risk means weighing how likely an effect is against how severe its consequences would be.
The total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.
Every stage from obtaining and processing the raw materials, through manufacture, packaging and transport, to use and finally disposal. All of these stages count towards the carbon footprint.
The carbon footprint can be reduced by reducing emissions of carbon dioxide and methane at any stage of the life cycle.

Using alternative energy supplies such as renewables or nuclear instead of fossil fuels; conserving energy and improving efficiency; capturing and storing carbon dioxide; taxes, licences and carbon offsetting such as planting trees; and reducing methane by keeping fewer livestock and by capturing the methane given off by landfill sites.

The cost of the changes; the technology not yet being available or developed on a large enough scale; the need for international cooperation, which is difficult to achieve; lack of public information and education; and people being unwilling to change their lifestyles.

misconceptions.question: Is the greenhouse effect a bad thing?
misconceptions.correct: The natural greenhouse effect keeps temperatures on Earth high enough to support life. The concern is the increase in greenhouse gases caused by human activity, not the effect itself.
misconceptions.misconception: The greenhouse effect is pollution damaging the planet, so we would be better off without any greenhouse gases at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase is nearly always met alongside global warming in the news, so students attach the word 'greenhouse' to harm and never meet the idea that the Earth would be frozen without it.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the two ideas: greenhouse gases in the atmosphere maintain temperatures high enough to support life; adding more of them raises the temperature further, and that is what causes concern.

misconceptions.question: Which radiation do greenhouse gases absorb?
misconceptions.correct: They absorb long wavelength radiation emitted by the warmed Earth. Short wavelength radiation from the Sun largely passes through the atmosphere to the surface.
misconceptions.misconception: Greenhouse gases block the Sun's rays, trapping the heat before it can get back out of the atmosphere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'trapped' in everyday descriptions suggests something is caught on the way in, and students rarely picture the Earth itself as a source of radiation.
misconceptions.correction: Follow the route: short wavelength in, absorbed by the surface, long wavelength out, and it is only the outgoing long wavelength radiation that greenhouse gases absorb and re-radiate.

misconceptions.question: Is the greenhouse effect caused by a hole in the ozone layer?
misconceptions.correct: The greenhouse effect is caused by greenhouse gases absorbing long wavelength radiation. It is a separate matter from the ozone layer, which is not part of this section.
misconceptions.misconception: Holes in the ozone layer let extra rays through, and that is what makes the Earth warm up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are 'atmosphere problems' met at the same time in primary science and in the media, so they merge into one story.
misconceptions.correction: Keep them apart. The greenhouse effect depends on long wavelength radiation leaving the Earth being absorbed by gases; it is not about anything letting extra radiation in.

misconceptions.question: Do greenhouse gases reflect radiation?
misconceptions.correct: They absorb long wavelength radiation and then re-radiate it in all directions, so only some of it returns to the surface.
misconceptions.misconception: The layer of greenhouse gases works like a mirror, bouncing all the radiation straight back down to the ground.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook diagrams draw a single arrow turning round at the top of the atmosphere, which looks exactly like reflection.
misconceptions.correction: Use the words absorb and re-radiate. The gas takes in the radiation and emits again in all directions, so some energy still escapes to space.

misconceptions.question: Is water vapour a greenhouse gas?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The specification names water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane as greenhouse gases.
misconceptions.misconception: Water vapour is just water in the air, so it cannot be a greenhouse gas like the pollutants are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate greenhouse gases with pollution, and water seems harmless and natural, so it is left off the list.
misconceptions.correction: Learn all three named gases together. Being natural does not stop a gas absorbing long wavelength radiation.

misconceptions.question: Are sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide greenhouse gases?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are atmospheric pollutants met elsewhere in the specification; the greenhouse gases named here are water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane.
misconceptions.misconception: Any harmful gas released when fuels burn adds to the greenhouse effect, so sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide must be greenhouse gases too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Combustion products are taught as one list of 'bad gases from burning fuels', so their different effects blur together.
misconceptions.correction: Sort the products of combustion by effect: carbon dioxide and water vapour are greenhouse gases, sulfur dioxide causes acid rain, and carbon monoxide is a toxic gas.

misconceptions.question: Does it matter which activity is paired with which gas?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Fossil fuel combustion and deforestation raise carbon dioxide; livestock farming, rice paddies and landfill waste raise methane.
misconceptions.misconception: Any activity that pollutes puts out both gases, so cattle farming and burning coal can be given as answers for either gas.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both gases are learnt in the same lesson as 'greenhouse gases from human activity', and the sources are not separated when revised.
misconceptions.correction: Build two short lists, one per gas, and check that each activity named actually releases the gas asked about.

misconceptions.question: Why does deforestation increase carbon dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: For two reasons: burning the felled timber releases carbon dioxide, and fewer trees remain to remove carbon dioxide from the air by photosynthesis.
misconceptions.misconception: Deforestation matters only because the wood is burned; once the burning stops there is no further effect.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The combustion route is visible and easy to picture, while the loss of a carbon dioxide sink is an absence rather than an event.
misconceptions.correction: State both routes in an answer: carbon dioxide added by burning, and carbon dioxide no longer removed by photosynthesis.

misconceptions.question: Does burning natural gas release methane into the atmosphere?
misconceptions.correct: No. Burning methane in a good supply of air produces carbon dioxide and water. The methane is used up, so this raises carbon dioxide, not methane.
misconceptions.misconception: Natural gas is methane, so burning it must add methane to the atmosphere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students track the fuel's name rather than the products of the reaction, and 'gas boiler' feels like a methane source.
misconceptions.correction: Write the combustion equation: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. The methane is a reactant and the greenhouse gases released are carbon dioxide and water vapour.

misconceptions.question: Is the scientific view on climate change just an opinion?
misconceptions.correct: It is based on peer-reviewed evidence: data published and checked by other scientists in the same field.
misconceptions.misconception: Scientists only 'believe' in climate change, so it is their opinion and one opinion is as good as another.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The specification's wording 'many scientists believe' is read as a personal belief, and media debate formats present two speakers as equal.
misconceptions.correction: Note what the belief rests on. The claim is judged by the quality of the peer-reviewed evidence behind it, not by who is asserting it.

misconceptions.question: If climate models are simplified, are they useless?
misconceptions.correct: No. Simplification means predictions carry uncertainty, but models built on measured data remain the best available guide to what may happen.
misconceptions.misconception: Climate is too complex to model, so any prediction is guesswork and can be ignored.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat 'uncertain' as meaning 'unknown', and hear differing predicted figures as evidence that nobody knows anything.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish uncertainty in the size of an effect from doubt that the effect exists. Models differ over how much, not over the direction of change.

misconceptions.question: Is a newspaper report as reliable as a scientific paper?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. Media reports may be simplified, may use only parts of the evidence, and may be biased; peer-reviewed work has been checked by other scientists.
misconceptions.misconception: If it has been printed with a graph and a quotation from a scientist, the report must be trustworthy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Real data quoted in a report looks like proof, and students are not used to asking what has been left out.
misconceptions.correction: Ask three questions of any report: who produced it, has it been peer reviewed, and does it show all the evidence or only the part that suits its argument.

misconceptions.question: Does a confident report with no uncertainty make the best evidence?
misconceptions.correct: No. Good scientific reporting states its uncertainties. A source that admits none is more likely to be selective or biased.
misconceptions.misconception: The strongest report is the one that gives a single clear answer and does not hedge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday life confidence reads as competence, so admitting uncertainty seems like weakness rather than honesty.
misconceptions.correction: When evaluating evidence, credit the report that describes its range of results and its limitations alongside its conclusion.

misconceptions.question: Who carries out peer review?
misconceptions.correct: Other scientists working in the same field, who check the work before it is published.
misconceptions.misconception: Peer review means the public, a government or the newspapers approve the findings.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'peer' is met in citizenship lessons as 'people like me', so students read it as public approval rather than expert scrutiny.
misconceptions.correction: Define peer as another expert in that field. Review happens before publication and is about checking method, data and conclusions.

misconceptions.question: Does climate change just mean everywhere gets hotter?
misconceptions.correct: An increase in average global temperature is a major cause of climate change, which means changes to long-term patterns of temperature, rainfall and weather worldwide.
misconceptions.misconception: Climate change means every place on Earth warms up by the same few degrees, so a cold winter disproves it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Global warming' is heard as a single number applied everywhere, and averages are not understood as hiding regional variation.
misconceptions.correction: Treat the rise as an average of the whole planet over time. Individual places and seasons may change by different amounts and in different directions.

misconceptions.question: Is acid rain an effect of global climate change?
misconceptions.correct: No. Acid rain is caused by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen. Potential effects of climate change include rising sea levels, more severe storms, changed rainfall patterns and changes to species distribution and food production.
misconceptions.misconception: Acid rain and a thinner ozone layer are on the list of things climate change does to the environment.
misconceptions.whyItArises: All the environmental topics are taught close together, so any environmental harm gets attached to climate change.
misconceptions.correction: Learn the four potential effects as a set tied to temperature and rainfall change, and keep acid rain and ozone as separate topics with separate causes.

misconceptions.question: Does a carbon footprint count only carbon dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted, so methane counts too.
misconceptions.misconception: It is called a carbon footprint, so only the carbon dioxide released is included in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name contains the word carbon, and methane is often taught in a separate part of the lesson from carbon footprints.
misconceptions.correction: Quote the definition in full: carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, over the full life cycle.

misconceptions.question: Which stages count towards a carbon footprint?
misconceptions.correct: Every stage of the full life cycle: raw materials, manufacture, transport, use and disposal.
misconceptions.misconception: The carbon footprint is what the product gives off while you are using it, so an electric appliance has almost none.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Emissions during use are visible and easy to imagine, while emissions in mining, manufacture and transport happen out of sight.
misconceptions.correction: Walk through the whole life cycle stage by stage and add the emissions at each one before deciding whether a product has a low footprint.

misconceptions.question: Do filters and scrubbers on chimneys reduce a carbon footprint?
misconceptions.correct: Not by themselves. Removing sulfur dioxide or particulates does not reduce emissions of carbon dioxide or methane, and it is those that determine the carbon footprint.
misconceptions.misconception: Any measure that cleans up what comes out of a chimney must cut the carbon footprint.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Reducing emissions' is treated as one idea, so measures aimed at different pollutants are assumed to work for all of them.
misconceptions.correction: Check which gas an action removes. Only actions that cut carbon dioxide or methane reduce the carbon footprint.

misconceptions.question: If we know how to cut emissions, why are they not cut?
misconceptions.correct: Actions may be limited by cost, by technology not yet being available at scale, by the difficulty of getting international cooperation, by lack of public information and education, and by people being unwilling to change their lifestyles.
misconceptions.misconception: Emissions could be stopped tomorrow if governments simply decided to, so there is no real reason for delay.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The chemistry of the solutions is straightforward, so the economic, technical and political barriers are invisible to students.
misconceptions.correction: Give a specific reason when asked why action is limited, such as the cost of replacing fossil fuel power stations or the need for agreement between many countries.

misconceptions.question: Does burning fuel warm the planet because it gives out heat?
misconceptions.correct: The warming comes from the carbon dioxide released, which absorbs long wavelength radiation leaving the surface. The heat released directly by the fire is not the mechanism.
misconceptions.misconception: All those fires, engines and power stations pour heat into the air, and that is what raises the Earth's temperature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Combustion is taught as an exothermic reaction, so the released energy is the obvious candidate for the warming.
misconceptions.correction: Link the activity to the gas, and the gas to the radiation. Fossil fuels matter because of the carbon dioxide they add to the atmosphere.

misconceptions.question: Does carbon dioxide sink and form a layer that traps heat?
misconceptions.correct: No. Gases in the atmosphere mix, and carbon dioxide warms the surface by absorbing long wavelength radiation and re-radiating it, not by forming a physical lid.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon dioxide is denser than air, so it settles into a layer above the ground that stops heat escaping.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students recall from practical work that carbon dioxide can be poured to extinguish a candle, and 'blanket' analogies suggest a physical covering.
misconceptions.correction: Describe the mechanism in terms of radiation absorbed and re-radiated by molecules spread through the atmosphere, not in terms of a layer of dense gas.

misconceptions.question: If the effects have not happened yet, is there any risk?
misconceptions.correct: The effects are potential, and because they would occur on a global scale even a modest probability carries serious environmental implications.
misconceptions.misconception: Nothing serious has happened so far, so the risk from climate change is essentially zero.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Risk is judged from personal experience, and consequences spread over decades and continents feel unreal compared with immediate hazards.
misconceptions.correction: Weigh likelihood against consequence. A global effect on sea level, weather and food supply is severe enough that even an uncertain prediction represents real risk.

misconceptions.question: Does uncertainty mean scientists disagree about whether warming is happening?
misconceptions.correct: No. Uncertainty is about how large and how fast the changes will be, not about whether the surface temperature is increasing.
misconceptions.misconception: Scientists say the evidence is uncertain, which means they are not sure the Earth is warming at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech 'uncertain' means 'not sure', so a technical statement about ranges of values is read as doubt about the whole idea.
misconceptions.correction: Describe uncertainty precisely: past temperatures estimated indirectly, short records, natural variation and simplified models all affect the size of the prediction.

misconceptions.question: Does cutting down trees raise carbon dioxide because there is less oxygen?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide rises because burning the timber releases it and because fewer trees remain to remove it by photosynthesis, not because it replaces missing oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: Trees make oxygen, so with fewer trees there is less oxygen and carbon dioxide simply fills the space left behind.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Photosynthesis is remembered as 'trees make oxygen' rather than as 'trees take in carbon dioxide', and gases are pictured as competing for room in a fixed container.
misconceptions.correction: Track the carbon dioxide itself: it is added by combustion and no longer removed by photosynthesis. Its amount does not depend on how much space the oxygen leaves.

misconceptions.question: Does global climate change alter what the air is made of?
misconceptions.correct: Its potential effects are on sea level, weather, rainfall, species distribution and food production. The proportions of nitrogen and oxygen in the air are not what changes.
misconceptions.misconception: Climate change means the atmosphere itself changes composition, so the amount of nitrogen or oxygen in the air drops.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The topic is taught immediately after the composition of the atmosphere, so 'changes to the atmosphere' is read as changes to the percentages of its main gases.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the small change in trace greenhouse gases, which is the cause, from the effects, which are changes in temperature, weather and the environment.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about greenhouse gases in the Earth's atmosphere is correct?

options.text: Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane are all greenhouse gases.
options.rationale: These are the three greenhouse gases named in the specification.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases but water vapour is not.
options.rationale: Water vapour seems natural and harmless, so students leave it off a list they associate with pollution.

options.text: Only gases released by human activity can act as greenhouse gases.
options.rationale: Students who think the greenhouse effect is pollution assume the gases must be man-made.

options.text: Greenhouse gases make up most of the atmosphere by volume.
options.rationale: A large effect is assumed to need a large amount of gas; in fact nitrogen and oxygen dominate the air.

mcqs.stem: A coal-fired power station releases carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, water vapour and nitrogen. Which two of these gases are greenhouse gases?

options.text: carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide
options.rationale: Sulfur dioxide is remembered as a harmful gas from burning fuels, so it is assumed to be a greenhouse gas.

options.text: sulfur dioxide and water vapour
options.rationale: Picks the pollutant over carbon dioxide, again confusing acid rain with the greenhouse effect.

options.text: carbon dioxide and water vapour
options.rationale: Both are named as greenhouse gases in the specification.

options.text: water vapour and nitrogen gas
options.rationale: Nitrogen is chosen because it is the most abundant gas in air, confusing abundance with greenhouse behaviour.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes how greenhouse gases keep the Earth's surface warm?

options.text: They absorb the short wavelength radiation coming from the Sun before it reaches the ground.
options.rationale: The idea that heat is 'trapped on the way in' is the commonest version of the effect students hold.

options.text: They absorb long wavelength radiation emitted by the Earth and re-radiate some of it back.
options.rationale: This is the greenhouse effect described in terms of the interaction of long wavelength radiation with matter.

options.text: They act as a mirror and reflect all the radiation from the Sun back to the surface.
options.rationale: Arrows turning round in textbook diagrams look like reflection rather than absorption and re-radiation.

options.text: They form a layer high up that blocks ultraviolet radiation coming from the Sun.
options.rationale: Confuses the greenhouse effect with the ozone layer, which the two topics being taught together encourages.

mcqs.stem: Radiation from the Sun falls on the Earth's surface. Which statement describes the radiation absorbed by the surface and the radiation it then emits?

options.text: It absorbs mainly long wavelength radiation and emits mainly short wavelength radiation.
options.rationale: Reverses the two steps, which follows from thinking greenhouse gases act on incoming sunlight.

options.text: It absorbs and then emits radiation of the same short wavelength as sunlight.
options.rationale: Assumes matter must re-emit exactly what it absorbs, so no change of wavelength occurs.

options.text: It absorbs and then emits radiation of the same long wavelength as infrared.
options.rationale: Treats the surface as simply bouncing infrared back, the reflection model applied to the ground.

options.text: It absorbs mainly short wavelength radiation and emits mainly long wavelength radiation.
options.rationale: Short wavelength radiation from the Sun is absorbed by matter at the surface, which then emits at longer wavelengths.

mcqs.stem: Burning more fossil fuels increases the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Why does this tend to raise the temperature at the Earth's surface?

options.text: More of the short wavelength radiation from the Sun is trapped inside the atmosphere.
options.rationale: Restates the popular 'trapping sunlight' account of the greenhouse effect.

options.text: More of the long wavelength radiation leaving the surface is absorbed and re-radiated back.
options.rationale: More greenhouse gas means more of the outgoing infrared is absorbed and re-radiated towards the surface.

options.text: The energy given out when the fossil fuels burn heats the whole atmosphere directly.
options.rationale: Combustion is known to be exothermic, so the released energy looks like the cause of the warming.

options.text: Carbon dioxide is denser than the air, so it settles into a low layer that stops heat escaping.
options.rationale: Draws on the demonstration of pouring carbon dioxide onto a candle plus the 'blanket' analogy.

mcqs.stem: Which of these human activities increases the amount of a greenhouse gas in the atmosphere?

options.text: planting new woodland on land that was previously farmed
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think any change to land use adds greenhouse gases; planting trees removes carbon dioxide.

options.text: fitting sulfur dioxide scrubbers to a coal-fired power station
options.rationale: Confuses sulfur dioxide with a greenhouse gas, so the action seems to change greenhouse gas amounts.

options.text: burning fossil fuels in power stations and vehicle engines
options.rationale: Combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas.

options.text: filtering solid particles out of waste water at a treatment works
options.rationale: Any pollution-related process is assumed to be linked to greenhouse gas emissions.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of human activities both increase the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?

options.text: burning fossil fuels for electricity, and cutting down forests
options.rationale: Both are activities named for carbon dioxide: combustion releases it and deforestation both releases it and reduces its removal.

options.text: keeping cattle for beef, and growing rice in flooded fields
options.rationale: Both of these raise methane, not carbon dioxide; students who learn one combined list pick them freely.

options.text: cutting down forests, and burying waste food in landfill sites
options.rationale: Half right, which is why it is tempting: landfill waste releases methane rather than carbon dioxide.

options.text: growing rice in flooded fields, and keeping herds of cattle
options.rationale: Again both are methane sources, chosen when the two gases are not separated in revision.

mcqs.stem: A large area of forest is cleared and the felled timber is burned. Why does this increase the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?

options.text: The burning releases carbon dioxide, but photosynthesis is not affected at all.
options.rationale: The visible combustion route is remembered while the loss of the carbon dioxide sink is overlooked.

options.text: Fewer trees means less oxygen, so carbon dioxide fills the space left.
options.rationale: Applies a 'gases swap places' idea instead of tracking where the carbon dioxide comes from.

options.text: The burning releases carbon dioxide, and fewer trees remain to take it in.
options.rationale: Deforestation acts in both ways: it adds carbon dioxide by combustion and removes a photosynthetic sink for it.

options.text: The bare soil reacts with rainwater and gives off carbon dioxide gas.
options.rationale: Invents a chemical route that sounds plausible after carbonate reactions have been taught.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of human activities both increase the amount of methane in the atmosphere?

options.text: burning natural gas in home boilers, and running petrol cars in cities
options.rationale: Natural gas is methane, so burning it is assumed to release methane; in fact it produces carbon dioxide and water.

options.text: raising cattle for meat and dairy, and growing rice in paddy fields
options.rationale: Livestock farming and flooded rice fields are both named sources of methane.

options.text: burning coal in power stations, and clearing areas of tropical forest
options.rationale: Both are carbon dioxide activities, chosen when the sources of the two gases are not separated.

options.text: growing rice in flooded paddy fields, and burning coal for electricity
options.rationale: Half right, so it attracts students who recognise one source and do not check the other.

mcqs.stem: Household waste is buried in a landfill site. Which greenhouse gas is released as the buried waste decomposes?

options.text: carbon dioxide, formed as the waste slowly burns
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide is the default answer for any greenhouse gas question, and 'burning' is assumed.

options.text: sulfur dioxide, formed from the sulfur in waste
options.rationale: Treats sulfur dioxide as a greenhouse gas released by any dirty process.

options.text: methane, formed as the buried waste decomposes
options.rationale: Decomposition of waste in landfill is a named human activity that increases atmospheric methane.

options.text: water vapour, formed as the warm waste dries
options.rationale: Water vapour is a greenhouse gas, so it is picked without checking the chemistry of decomposition.

mcqs.stem: Many scientists believe that human activities will cause the temperature of the Earth's atmosphere to increase at the surface. On what is this belief based?

options.text: on evidence that has been peer reviewed by other scientists in the field
options.rationale: The specification states that the position is based on peer-reviewed evidence.

options.text: on the personal opinions held by individual scientists who work on climate
options.rationale: The word 'believe' is read as personal belief rather than a conclusion drawn from evidence.

options.text: on computer models that predict future climate with total certainty
options.rationale: Overstates what models do; students assume a prediction is only valid if it is certain.

options.text: on governments around the world voting to accept the conclusion
options.rationale: Confuses acceptance by authority with scrutiny by other scientists.

mcqs.stem: Global climate is a very complex system. What difficulty does this create for scientists?

options.text: Models cannot be tested at all, so their output is only opinion.
options.rationale: Treats any simplification as making a model worthless.

options.text: Models are not needed, because past temperature records are complete.
options.rationale: Assumes direct measurements exist for the whole of the past, ignoring the uncertainty in old data.

options.text: Models must be kept private until every scientist agrees the results.
options.rationale: Misreads peer review as requiring unanimous agreement before publication.

options.text: Models have to be simplified, so their predictions carry uncertainty.
options.rationale: The specification states that the difficulty of modelling such complex systems leads to simplified models.

mcqs.stem: A newspaper article about climate change quotes one graph from a single study and gives no other data. Which criticism of the article is valid?

options.text: It must be wrong, because newspapers never report science correctly.
options.rationale: Swaps uncritical trust for blanket distrust; the source alone does not make data false.

options.text: It may use only part of the evidence, giving a biased impression.
options.rationale: Media reports may be based on only parts of the evidence and may be biased, as the specification states.

options.text: It is reliable, because a graph shows data and data cannot mislead.
options.rationale: Real data presented selectively still looks like proof to students.

options.text: It is reliable, because journalists check their work before printing.
options.rationale: Confuses editorial checking with peer review by scientists in the field.

mcqs.stem: Two reports about global climate change are compared. Which feature gives the better reason to trust one of the reports?

options.text: Its data were collected over many years and checked by other scientists.
options.rationale: Long-run data that has been peer reviewed is stronger evidence than a single unchecked source.

options.text: It presents a single clear conclusion and does not mention any uncertainty.
options.rationale: Confidence is mistaken for quality, whereas good reporting states its uncertainties.

options.text: It appeared in a national newspaper that is read by millions of people.
options.rationale: Treats a wide readership as a check on accuracy.

options.text: It was funded by a company that works in the industry it is describing.
options.rationale: Students may read industry funding as expertise rather than as a possible source of bias.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes an uncertainty in the evidence base for global climate change?

options.text: The amount of carbon dioxide in today's atmosphere cannot be measured accurately.
options.rationale: Assumes uncertainty about the future means present-day quantities are unknown too.

options.text: Scientists have no evidence of any kind about climate before the 1900s.
options.rationale: Turns limited or indirect evidence into no evidence at all.

options.text: Temperatures from long ago are estimated indirectly rather than measured.
options.rationale: The further back the record goes, the less direct the measurement, which limits how precisely past climate is known.

options.text: Uncertainty means scientists disagree over whether warming is happening.
options.rationale: Reads the everyday meaning of 'uncertain' into a statement about ranges of values.

mcqs.stem: A scientist submits results on climate change for publication in a journal. What happens when the results are peer reviewed?

options.text: Members of the public vote on whether they accept the conclusions drawn.
options.rationale: Reads 'peer' as 'ordinary people' rather than 'expert in the same field'.

options.text: The scientists who did the work read it through once more themselves.
options.rationale: Misses the point that the checking must be independent of the original team.

options.text: Other scientists in the same field check the work before it is published.
options.rationale: Peer review is scrutiny by experts in the field prior to publication, which helps detect errors and false claims.

options.text: A newspaper editor decides whether the findings are interesting enough to print.
options.rationale: Confuses publication in the media with publication in a scientific journal.

mcqs.stem: Why is it important that results about global climate change are communicated to a wide range of audiences?

options.text: So that scientists no longer need to publish their results in journals.
options.rationale: Sets public communication against peer-reviewed publication instead of alongside it.

options.text: So the public and decision makers can act on what the evidence shows.
options.rationale: Communicating beyond the scientific community allows informed decisions to be made about how to respond.

options.text: So that the findings become correct once enough people accept them.
options.rationale: Treats scientific conclusions as decided by popularity rather than by evidence.

options.text: So that only the scientists who agree with the results will read them.
options.rationale: Inverts the purpose of communication, which is to reach people beyond the field.

mcqs.stem: Which change is described as a major cause of climate change?

options.text: an increase in the average global temperature
options.rationale: The specification states that an increase in average global temperature is a major cause of climate change.

options.text: an increase in temperature at every place on Earth
options.rationale: Reads a global average as a uniform rise everywhere.

options.text: a decrease in the amount of water vapour in the air
options.rationale: Water vapour is not treated as a greenhouse gas, so removing it is imagined to cause change.

options.text: an increase in the total mass of gas in the atmosphere
options.rationale: Assumes that adding gases matters because of the extra mass rather than their absorption of radiation.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a potential effect of global climate change?

options.text: acid rain damaging trees and buildings across large areas of land
options.rationale: Acid rain is a separate environmental topic caused by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen.

options.text: the ozone layer becoming thicker above the polar regions
options.rationale: Ozone and the greenhouse effect are merged into a single 'atmosphere problem'.

options.text: sea levels rising, causing more flooding of low-lying land
options.rationale: Rising sea level, with flooding and coastal erosion, is one of the potential effects to be described briefly.

options.text: the amount of nitrogen in the atmosphere falling sharply
options.rationale: Assumes that a change in the air must mean a change in its main constituent.

mcqs.stem: Global climate change may alter the temperature and rainfall patterns of a farming region. Which effect on that region is most likely?

options.text: changes to the number of daylight hours the region receives each year
options.rationale: Confuses climate with the astronomical causes of day length and the seasons.

options.text: changes to the crops that can be grown there, affecting food production
options.rationale: Changed temperature and rainfall alter which crops a region can support, one of the potential effects of climate change.

options.text: changes to the proportion of nitrogen in the air above the farmland
options.rationale: Assumes climate change alters the composition of the air rather than the weather.

options.text: changes to the acidity of the rain because more fuel is being burned
options.rationale: Brings acid rain in as an effect of climate change instead of a separate pollution topic.

mcqs.stem: A student says there is no need to worry about global climate change because the predicted effects have not happened yet. Which response best describes the risk?

options.text: The effects are certain to happen, so there is no real uncertainty at all.
options.rationale: Overcorrects the student by claiming certainty the specification does not; the effects are potential.

options.text: The effects would be local, so only countries near the equator are at risk.
options.rationale: Shrinks the scale of the problem so that the risk seems to apply to other people.

options.text: The effects cannot be predicted, so the risk cannot be discussed usefully.
options.rationale: Uses the uncertainty in the models as a reason to dismiss the question entirely.

options.text: The effects would be worldwide, so even an uncertain risk is a serious one.
options.rationale: Judging risk means weighing likelihood against the scale and severity of the consequences, which here are global.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the carbon footprint of a product?

options.text: the total carbon dioxide emitted over the life cycle, but no other gases
options.rationale: The word 'carbon' in the name suggests that only carbon dioxide is counted.

options.text: the total carbon dioxide emitted while the product is actually being used
options.rationale: Emissions during use are the visible ones, so the rest of the life cycle is forgotten.

options.text: the mass of carbon compounds that the finished product itself contains
options.rationale: Reads 'carbon footprint' as something inside the product rather than something emitted.

options.text: the total carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over its life cycle
options.rationale: This is the definition given in the specification.

mcqs.stem: The carbon footprint of a cotton shirt is being worked out. Which emissions should be included?

options.text: those from growing the cotton, making, transporting and disposing of the shirt
options.rationale: The carbon footprint covers the full life cycle, from raw material to disposal.

options.text: those from making the shirt in the factory, and from nothing else at all
options.rationale: Manufacture is the stage students picture, so the rest of the life cycle is left out.

options.text: those from transporting the finished shirt from the factory to the shops
options.rationale: 'Food miles' style reasoning makes transport feel like the whole of a footprint.

options.text: those of carbon dioxide only, since the other gases contain no carbon
options.rationale: Excludes methane despite methane, CH4, containing carbon and being a greenhouse gas.

mcqs.stem: How can the carbon footprint of a product be reduced?

options.text: by measuring the emissions more carefully at each stage of its life cycle
options.rationale: Confuses measuring a quantity with changing it; better data does not lower emissions.

options.text: by removing all of the carbon compounds from the materials it is made of
options.rationale: Treats the footprint as the carbon held in the product rather than the gases emitted.

options.text: by fitting filters so that the waste gases leave higher up in the air
options.rationale: Assumes any chimney treatment reduces the footprint, when the gases are still released.

options.text: by reducing the emissions of carbon dioxide and methane during its life cycle
options.rationale: The specification states that the carbon footprint can be reduced by reducing emissions of carbon dioxide and methane.

mcqs.stem: Which action would reduce emissions of methane?

options.text: fitting filters to power station chimneys to trap the waste gases
options.rationale: Chimney treatment is assumed to cut all emissions, but power stations are not a methane source.

options.text: collecting the gas given off by landfill sites and using it as a fuel
options.rationale: Capturing the methane given off by decomposing waste stops it being released into the atmosphere, so methane emissions fall.

options.text: burning more natural gas instead of coal in the power stations
options.rationale: Burning natural gas is thought to release methane; in fact it consumes it and releases carbon dioxide.

options.text: growing more rice in flooded paddy fields to absorb the gas
options.rationale: Reverses a known methane source into a supposed remedy, treating plants as a sink for any gas.

mcqs.stem: Governments agree that emissions of carbon dioxide should fall, but in many countries they stay high. Which reason best explains why the action taken is limited?

options.text: Emissions must stay high because greenhouse gases are needed for life.
options.rationale: Misapplies the fact that the natural greenhouse effect supports life to defend further emissions.

options.text: Scientists do not yet know which gases cause the greenhouse effect.
options.rationale: Treats scientific uncertainty about the size of the effect as ignorance about its cause.

options.text: Carbon dioxide cannot be produced in smaller amounts by any method.
options.rationale: Assumes the barrier is chemical rather than economic, technical and political.

options.text: Changing to alternative energy supplies is expensive and takes many years.
options.rationale: Cost and the time needed to replace existing technology on a national scale are genuine reasons why action is limited.
